summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would replace the current VET FEE-HELP loan scheme with a new student loan program for vocational education and training starting on 1 January 2017.

Under the new program, the Commonwealth would approve student loans only for eligible students in approved courses, and providers would face stricter entry requirements, including a ban on using intermediaries to recruit students for loans.
Initial loan caps would be set at $5,000, $10,000, and $15,000, with the Minister able to exempt courses with high delivery costs.
changes: The bill would introduce loan caps for eligible courses.
The bill would strengthen compliance and governance by allowing the Commonwealth to suspend providers immediately in urgent cases and withhold payments to non-compliant providers.
The bill would ban brokers or agents from recruiting students for loans and require student consent before providers can contact them about loan availability.
The bill would require all existing VET FEE-HELP providers to re-apply for approval under the new program, with some exemptions for certain bodies like TAFEs.
The bill would impose an application fee for providers and an annual levy through the accompanying Charges Bill.
The bill would require students to log in periodically to confirm active enrolment from 1 July 2017.
summary.affected: Students, vocational education and training providers, and the Commonwealth are affected.

divisions.question: The majority voted against an [amendment](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2016-10-18.8.3) to the motion "*That this bill be now read a [second time](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html)*", which means it was rejected. This motion was to condemn the Government's handling of the [VET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocational_education) FEE-HELP scheme. ### Some more context This motion was introduced during a debate about three bills. Together, the bills [replace the VET FEE-HELP loan scheme](http://www.abc.net.au/triplej/programs/hack/crackdown-on-private-college-loans/7902640). These changes include: * limiting student loans to eligible students for approved courses; * introducing stronger eligibility requirements; * banning providers from using brokers or agents to interact or engage with students in relation to the loans; and * introducing civil penalties, infringement notices, enforceable undertakings and injunctions. Read more on the [Department of Education & Training](https://www.education.gov.au/vet-fee-help-reforms) website. ### Motion text > *That all the words after “That” be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *“whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House condemns the Government’s failure to properly administer the VET FEE-HELP scheme, leaving taxpayers and students to deal with the consequences of their mismanagement.”*

The majority voted against [amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2016-10-19.108.2) to the bill that were introduced by Labor MP [Kate Ellis](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/adelaide/kate_ellis), which means they were unsuccessful. ### What are these bills all about? These three bills [replace the VET FEE-HELP loan scheme](http://www.abc.net.au/triplej/programs/hack/crackdown-on-private-college-loans/7902640). These changes include: * limiting student loans to eligible students for approved courses; * introducing stronger eligibility requirements; * banning providers from using brokers or agents to interact or engage with students in relation to the loans; and * introducing civil penalties, infringement notices, enforceable undertakings and injunctions. Read more on the [Department of Education & Training](https://www.education.gov.au/vet-fee-help-reforms) website. ### What were the amendments? The amendments would introduce a [VET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocational_education) Student Loans [Ombudsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ombudsman). The Coalition Government voted against the amendment but Liberal MP [Karen Andrews](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/mcpherson/karen_andrews) said [in her contribution](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2016-10-19.109.1): > *As I noted in my second reading speech on this bill, the government intends to establish an ombudsman. This will increase student protections and provide a further avenue for dispute resolution. I note that Labor never provided an ombudsman when it established or expanded the VET FEE-HELP scheme. Stakeholders have raised a number of different models for an ombudsman, which the government is currently considering. So, whilst it supports the principle of an ombudsman, it will not support the opposition's amendment.* ### Amendment text See the text of these amendments on [OpenAustralia](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2016-10

speeches.speaker: Karen Andrews
speeches.brief: The bill ends the VET FEE-HELP scheme, establishes transition arrangements for current students and providers, and makes consequential amendments to three related acts.

speeches.speaker: Karen Andrews
speeches.brief: The speaker moved the second reading of the VET Student Loans (Charges) Bill 2016, which enables the Commonwealth to charge approved VET Student Loans program providers an annual charge.

speeches.speaker: Kate Ellis
speeches.brief: Labor offered in-principle support for the VET Student Loans Bill 2016 but condemned the government's failure to administer the VET FEE-HELP scheme, citing a 400% blowout, billions wasted, five ministers in three years, and exploitation of vulnerable students, while noting the government had copied Labor's policies.

speeches.speaker: Julian Leeser
speeches.brief: The VET Student Loans Bill 2016 was supported as a fix for the VET FEE-HELP scheme, citing cost blowouts from $325 million in 2012 to $2.9 billion in 2015, completion rates of 22.9% overall and 7.8% for online students, and widespread exploitation of vulnerable students. The new scheme introduces stricter provider checks, a stepped loan cap, and course lists linked to skills priorities, with projected cuts of $2.4 billion in annual loans and $25 billion in HELP debt over 10 years, plus automatic entry for TAFEs such as Hornsby TAFE.

speeches.speaker: Julian Leeser
speeches.brief: The VET Student Loans Bill 2016 bans third-party brokers and agents from recruiting students and limits subcontracting, introducing stronger compliance measures including monitoring, civil penalties, and suspension powers. The bill aims to protect students from unethical practices, restore integrity to the VET sector, and reduce government debt.

speeches.speaker: Julian Hill
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government's VET Student Loans Bill 2016 is overdue and copies Labor's policies after four years of inaction, noting that graduation rates for the 10 largest providers were under five per cent in 2014, wasting $900 million in taxpayer money. They criticised the bill for not going far enough on regulating education agents and for lacking measures to restore $2.75 billion cut from TAFE and apprenticeships.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Price
speeches.brief: The Turnbull government introduced the VET Student Loans Bill 2016 to replace the VET FEE-HELP scheme, which had cost taxpayers $2.9 billion by 2015 and seen student loans increase by 792%. The new program includes annual levies on providers, loan caps of $5,000, $10,000 and $15,000, restrictions on eligible courses, a ban on brokers and unsolicited student contact, and stronger compliance powers.

speeches.speaker: Milton Dick
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the VET Student Loans Bill 2016 amendment, citing $3 billion in unrecoverable loans, graduation rates under 5% for the 10 largest providers costing $215,000 per graduate, and a 53.6% drop in apprenticeships in Oxley since 2013. They criticised the government for inaction and called for federal-state cooperation on TAFE funding.

speeches.speaker: Keith Pitt
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the VET Student Loans Bill 2016 was needed to replace Labor's failed VET-FEE HELP scheme, citing a 792% loan increase from $325 million in 2012 to $2.9 billion in 2015 and examples of predatory providers using misleading job ads and offering free iPads. The bill introduces an approved course list aligned with industry needs, loan caps of $5,000, $10,000 and $15,000, a ban on brokers and cold-calling, and a seven-year provider approval limit.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wallace
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the VET Student Loans Bill 2016 is essential to replace Labor's failed VET FEE-HELP scheme, which grew from $325 million in 2012 to $2.9 billion in 2015, and to introduce tighter controls including loan caps of $5,000, $10,000 and $15,000, a ban on brokers, and a focus on courses aligned with industry needs.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Bird
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the amendment to the VET Student Loans Bill 2016, arguing the government failed to act quickly enough on VET FEE-HELP abuses as the scheme's cost blew out from $700 million to $3 billion under its watch, and called for a sector-wide review, reinvestment of savings, and support for TAFE and apprenticeships.

speeches.speaker: Darren Chester
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Vet Student Loans Bill 2016, encouraging students not to be defined by their ATAR scores and citing their own success without a university degree.

speeches.speaker: Ross Hart
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the government’s VET Student Loans Bill adopts long-standing Labor policy after a "backflip," but fails to provide redress for students defrauded by unscrupulous providers. They criticised the exclusion of over 60 creative arts courses from loan eligibility, citing concerns over inadequate consultation and potential harm to Tasmania’s arts communities, and noted that the bill lacks provision for a VET loans ombudsman.

speeches.speaker: Chris Crewther
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the VET Student Loans Bill 2016 and associated bills, arguing they would replace the flawed VET FEE-HELP scheme with tougher provider entry criteria, a list of 347 eligible courses (478 removed), and measures to protect students and taxpayers. The speaker also noted Dunkley's 3.6% economic growth and falling unemployment, and cited Phoenix Institute's revocation for inducements and a 4% graduation rate.

speeches.speaker: Emma McBride
speeches.brief: The speaker criticised the Coalition government's handling of the VET sector, citing widespread rorts and a lack of regulation that left students with large debts and no qualifications, and argued that Labor's proposed reforms—including an ombudsman, loan caps, and a TAFE funding guarantee—were copied by the government after years of inaction. Specific figures included Evocca College receiving $200 million in VET FEE-HELP funds with only a 25% completion rate, and VET FEE-HELP debt rising from $700 million in 2013 to $2.9 billion in 2015.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: The coalition government is fixing Labor's VET FEE-HELP scheme, which saw loan values blow out from $26 million to $2.9 billion and completion rates at only 22%. The VET Student Loans Bill introduces tougher provider criteria, bans brokers, caps loans at $5,000–$15,000 per course, and allows ministerial exemptions for high-cost courses like aviation.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the VET Student Loans bills, which replace the VET FEE-HELP scheme from 1 January 2017 with loan caps of $5,000, $10,000 and $15,000, new student eligibility checks, and powers to suspend noncompliant providers. He also criticised the government for failing to act earlier on provider misconduct and for cutting $2.5 billion from skills and training, including $1 billion from apprenticeships, with apprentice numbers falling from 417,700 to 295,300 between 2013 and 2015.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: The Turnbull government's mismanagement and incompetence caused widespread rorting in the VET student loans program, with figures including a 417% increase in students at Australian Careers Network to 25,784, and growth in payments to Careers Australia from $3.5 million to $108 million and Evocca from $24.9 million to $131 million; an estimated 40% of VET debts will never be repaid. The speaker argued the government was asleep at the wheel, delayed action until a Senate inquiry, and is now adopting Labor’s proposed reforms, including the need for an ombudsman.
